searches.note: Thirty three searches of a share of forty five, twelve left unspent, none of them the author's. Fifteen were restricted to a primary domain (Viña Don Melchor twice, the company's filings twice, Almaviva five times, Santa Rita three times, the Consejo de Monumentos Nacionales, Cousiño Macul, and Viñedo Chadwick with Errázuriz once), and one to the importers' sheets of Viñedo Chadwick; three were spent in vain on the kultrun. No WebFetch was tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a detail stood on one page that is not the house speaking of itself, it was cut or said with less; the houses' own claims stay told as their accounts.
Critics' and writers' own sites met among the results are cited neither in the fragment nor here; the living met are listed below, described in the records, never named.
The serving temperatures follow the Codex's service reference: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius for all five full reds; no air is promised to soften tannin.
The edits were made in place by exact string replacement, keeping the author's layout, and linted sound with five records refuted.

tested: The founder and his dates: born in Santiago on 10 October 1833 by the parliamentary library (1834 in the company's visitor guide), died 1892; lawyer, deputy and senator, minister of finance from 7 January 1869 to 2 August 1870 (BCN, Wikipedia). Sound, except Liberal, which no source read gave.
The founding: 1883 at Pirque on property owned by his wife, Emiliana Subercaseaux (the 20-F of 2010 and 2019, the house's history). Sound, worded as the filings say.

Bordeaux varieties and the French oenologist, M. de Labouchère, overseeing the planting and the first harvest: the company's 20-F. Sound as the company's account; its clause that the varieties came before phylloxera ruined France is cut.

1921 and 1933: the deed of incorporation of 31 December 1921 converting the family firm into a stock company with shares for every family member, those shares traded on the Santiago exchange from 1933 (20-F 2018 and 2019, annual report 2006; Wikipedia gives 1923 and a student essay 1921). Changed: the house did not leave family hands in 1921.

1984, Peynaud and the collaborator: Viña Don Melchor's timeline says Peynaud tasted a Puente Alto Cabernet in 1984 and proposed his collaborator to lead the project. Changed from samples taken to Bordeaux.
1987 first vintage, 1997 parcel by parcel, 2019 Viña Don Melchor of its own: the house's timeline and pages, a Concha y Toro presentation, The Peak, Wine Industry Advisor. Sound.

The vineyard: north bank of the Maipo at about 650 metres, seven main parcels of Cabernet, Parcel 1 the oldest, planted in 1979, own rooted massal selection (Viña Don Melchor's pages and sheets). Sound. Lots: 142 or 151 sub-parcels, more than a hundred, against the record's some two hundred. Changed.

Making: fifteen months in French oak, 72 per cent new in 2019 and 71 in 2020 (the house's sheets). Sound. DM/01 2022: 88 per cent Cabernet Sauvignon and 12 Cabernet Franc, mainly from Parcel 1. Others changed to mainly.

Label: D.O. Puente Alto on every sheet read. Sound. Glass, ageing and service: within the house's notes and the Codex's service reference (full red, 16 to 18). Cards and questions: one right answer each, distractors of one kind, the explanations teach. Rules: nobody living named, no price, score or volatile figure, British, no dash.

tested: The 1997 agreement between Baroness Philippine de Rothschild and the chairman of Concha y Toro (the house's history page). Sound; the chairman stays described.

First vintage 1996 and launch in 1998: the house's history frames the first vintage as launched in 1998 and its vintage list shows the 1996 (75 per cent Cabernet Sauvignon, 19 Carménère, 6 Cabernet Franc, sixteen months in new French oak). Sound.
The winery: designed by a Chilean architect, native woods from the south, a roof whose curves echo the Andes (the house's page); built in 1998 and opened in 2000 in one account only. Years cut.

The label: Almaviva in Beaumarchais's own handwriting and three reproductions of a stylised design, a vision of the earth and the cosmos (the house, in English and Spanish); Mapuche by Grand Cru Wijnen; kultrun by Lea and Sandeman alone, in three searches. Changed to a stylised Mapuche design.
Grapes: the house's vintage list (2000 Cabernet Sauvignon and Carménère only; 2017 and 2019 with Merlot; Petit Verdot in most recent years, absent from 2005 and 2008). Changed.

Making: the must cooled on its skins, then warmed for fermentation in steel tanks sized to each parcel with a final maceration; spontaneous malolactic; about ten months in the Grand Chai and six to eight more in the second year cellar; sixteen to twenty months, 73 per cent new in 2023 (the house's winemaking page and sheets). Sound.
Sites: 65 hectares reserved for Almaviva at Puente Alto, oldest vines of 1978 (the house's terroir page). Sound as told.

Story beats otherwise: Baron Philippe (1902 to 1988), Philippine (1933 to 2014) succeeding him in 1988, Opus One with the Mondavi family, Epu as the Mapuche word for two, the three French ventures and Carménère. Sound by the Codex's own records and the author's sources; not searched again.
Cards and questions: one right answer each; the red pepper question offers no Cabernet Franc, so Carménère is the one key. Rules: sound.

tested: Founding in 1880 by Domingo Fernández Concha (the library, the house's reports, several accounts; one gives 1881 for the start of the main house). Sound; the founder stays described.

The García Huidobro years, from the end of the nineteenth century to the middle of the 1970s, beginning with Vicente García Huidobro, the founder's son in law, under the family's ownership (the house's annual reports). Changed from run to belonged.
1980: the Claro group, with Owens Illinois, bought part of the winery, full ownership in 1988 (the house's reports, fact sheet). Sound as bought into.

1972: Supreme Decree 2017 of 24 October 1972 declared the park, the main house, Paula Jaraquemada's house, the chapel and the cellars a historic monument (the Consejo de Monumentos Nacionales). Changed from the headquarters.

The 120: the house's fact sheet says 120 patriots took refuge in 1814 in Paula Jaraquemada's home; the council's record says the hacienda sheltered 120 patriot soldiers under San Martín after Cancha Rayada in 1818; Memoria Chilena tells her sheltering of the patriot army at her Paine hacienda after Cancha Rayada. Changed: Rancagua out, both years told.
Paula Jaraquemada: born in Santiago on 18 June 1768, died 7 September 1851 (Memoria Chilena, Wikipedia). Sound.

Casa Real: first vintage 1989, fermented in large wooden casks then, stainless steel since; 100 per cent Cabernet Sauvignon; Wine Legend (Decanter). Sound. The block: Carneros Viejo by the house's page and Decanter, with a second sector planted in the 1970s and 1980s in one account, ungrafted massal selections (International First Growths). Changed.

Barrels: the house's pages read give no months; the author's merchants stand for 2018 onwards; most new no longer covers the 2000s. The French barrels of the mid 1980s and the winemakers' years of watching the block: in no source read, cut.
Questions: the story question keyed a year the monuments council gives otherwise, so it now asks who the 120 were. Rules: the house's winemakers met in the results are not named; sound.

picks: All five picks stand, and no swap was proposed: Concha y Toro's Don Melchor, Almaviva, Santa Rita's Casa Real, Cousiño Macul's Lota and Viñedo Chadwick are the Maipo houses and wines a sommelier meets first, three of them from Puente Alto.

For the read-together agent: the plan's why for Santa Rita says its cellars are said to have sheltered 120 patriots in 1814; the house's fact sheet says Paula Jaraquemada's home, and the monuments council says 1818, so the why might read that the estate, by its account, sheltered 120 patriots.

For the read-together agent: the plan's why for Cousiño Macul says held by one family since its founding; that is the house's claim on its history page and may stand as history, but it speaks of the present.
